question_text: Underline the changes in the field of society and economy from the Rig Vedic to the later Vedic period. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: From Rig Vedic to later Vedic society
topics: From Rig Vedic to later Vedic society
keyPointers: The Rig Vedic world was tribal, pastoral and relatively open
The later Vedic world was agricultural, graded and settled
Society hardened into varna; the economy hardened into land and iron
The change is from a moving camp to a territorial kingdom

points.text: The move from the Rig Vedic to the later Vedic age is a move from a cattle camp to a settled agrarian order.
Kinship and a fluid varna gave way to a stricter status. The position of women narrowed, and rituals grew longer and more priestly.
Pasture gave way to plough agriculture, iron tools and a surplus that could support a territorial king.
Society became more ranked, and the economy became a land economy. Both changes belong to the same settlement.

question_text: Estimate the contribution of Pallavas of Kanchi for the development of art and literature of South India. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Pallavas of Kanchi in art and literature
topics: Pallavas of Kanchi in art and literature
keyPointers: Kanchi under the Pallavas became a school, not only a capital
Rock-cut halls led on to structural stone temples
Sanskrit and Tamil both flourished at the same court
The later South Indian temple style begins here

points.text: The Pallavas of Kanchi turned the northern Tamil country into a centre that the rest of the south copied.
Mahendravarman and his successors cut cave temples and then built structural temples at Mahabalipuram and Kanchi, with a new sculpture of the divine and the royal.
Sanskrit kavya and Tamil devotional verse were both patronised, so the court held a classical and a popular literature together.
Their contribution is the model: a stone temple and a bilingual literary culture that the Cholas inherited.

question_text: What were the events that led to the Quit India Movement? Point out its results. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Events and results of Quit India
topics: Events and results of Quit India
keyPointers: The failure of the Cripps offer and the threat of a Japanese advance brought the call
The movement was leaderless within hours and still nationwide
It did not expel the British in 1942
It made a return to the old constitution politically impossible

points.text: Quit India was called when the war, a failed negotiation and the fear of invasion came together in 1942.
The Cripps Mission offered too little. The Congress would not fight as a dependent party, and Gandhi asked Britain to leave.
The leaders were jailed at once. Strikes, attacks on rail and a parallel authority in some districts followed, and were put down hard.
The immediate result was repression. The lasting result was that India would not be governed after the war on the old terms.

question_text: What is sea surface temperature rise? How does it affect the formation of tropical cyclones? (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Sea surface temperature and tropical cyclones
topics: Sea surface temperature and tropical cyclones
keyPointers: Sea surface temperature is the warmth of the top layer of the ocean
A cyclone is an engine that runs on that warmth
A warmer sea gives more moisture and a lower pressure to start from
A storm that forms can intensify faster

points.text: Sea surface temperature rise is the warming of the ocean's upper layer, now being driven by a hotter climate.
A tropical cyclone needs warm water, moist air and a spin. Water above about 26 degrees supplies the evaporation that feeds the storm.
A higher temperature increases that fuel, so storms form more readily in a longer season and can strengthen more quickly.
The rise does not create every cyclone. It loads the ones that form.

question_text: Why do large cities tend to attract more migrants than smaller towns? Discuss in the light of conditions in developing countries. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Why large cities draw more migrants
topics: Why large cities draw more migrants
keyPointers: A large city offers more kinds of work than a small town
Services, a hospital and a college are concentrated there
In a developing country the village pushes and the primate city pulls
The migrant often accepts a slum because the alternative pays less

points.text: Large cities attract more migrants because they hold more jobs, more services and more chances of a second start.
In developing countries a few cities dominate industry, trade and the state, while small towns have thin markets.
Rural distress and a weak local town push people toward the one place they have heard will hire.
The attraction is rational and unequal. The city grows faster than it can house the people it calls.

question_text: What is the phenomenon of 'cloudbursts'? Explain. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: What a cloudburst is
topics: What a cloudburst is
keyPointers: A cloudburst is an extreme rain over a very small area in a very short time
Moist air is forced up a slope and dumps its water at once
Hills turn that rain into a flash flood
The event is local, which is why a warning often arrives late

points.text: A cloudburst is a sudden, very heavy fall of rain over a few square kilometres, often in the hills.
Warm moist air is lifted sharply by a mountain or a thundercloud, cools, and releases its water in minutes rather than hours.
A steep valley cannot hold that volume, so the rain becomes a flash flood and a debris flow.
The phenomenon is meteorological. The disaster is what the slope does with the water.

question_text: What is the concept of a 'demographic winter'? Is the world moving towards such a situation? Elaborate. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Demographic winter
topics: Demographic winter
keyPointers: Demographic winter is a lasting fall of births below replacement
Some rich countries and a few Asian ones are already there
The whole world is not; many regions are still young
The question is whether low fertility spreads faster than population momentum fades

points.text: A demographic winter is a society whose births stay so low that it ages and, in time, shrinks.
Parts of Europe, East Asia and a few others already have fertility well below replacement and a rising share of the old.
Much of Africa and parts of South Asia are still young. The world average is falling, but it is not one winter.
The world is moving toward lower fertility. It is not yet a single demographic winter.

question_text: Distinguish between gender equality, gender equity and women's empowerment. Why is it important to take gender concerns into account in programme design and implementation? (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Equality, equity and women's empowerment
topics: Equality, equity and women's empowerment
keyPointers: Equality is the same rule. Equity is a fair result. Empowerment is the power to use either
A programme that ignores the difference treats unequal people as if they started equal
Design decides who can reach the benefit
Implementation decides whether she actually receives it

points.text: Gender equality gives the same right. Equity adjusts the means so the right can be used. Empowerment is the woman being able to decide.
A scheme that ignores unpaid care, safety and a male gatekeeper will be equal on paper and unused in practice.
Design must ask who cannot travel, who does not own a phone, and who is not allowed to attend. Implementation must check that the benefit reached her.
Gender concerns are not an extra chapter. They are how a programme fails or works.

question_text: Intercaste marriages between castes which have socio-economic parity have increased, to some extent, but this is less true of interreligious marriages. Discuss. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Intercaste and interreligious marriage
topics: Intercaste and interreligious marriage
keyPointers: Caste can bend when class matches. Religion is treated as a harder line
Education and the city make a same-status intercaste match thinkable
A religious boundary carries family, law and a public hostility
The rise is real and still small

points.text: Marriage in India is loosening inside class more easily than it is loosening across religion.
Where two castes share education and income, an intercaste match can be absorbed as a family decision.
An interreligious match is read as a change of side. Law, a hostile public and the family resist it more.
Parity has opened a narrow gate between castes. It has not opened the same gate between religions.

question_text: In dealing with socio-economic issues of development, what kind of collaboration between government, NGOs and private sector would be most productive? (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Collaboration of state, NGO and private sector
topics: Collaboration of state, NGO and private sector
keyPointers: The state sets the right and the rule
The NGO reaches the person the office does not
The private sector brings a method and a scale, not the purpose
The productive form is a clear role for each, not a blurred partnership

points.text: The most productive collaboration gives each party the work it is actually good at.
Government holds the mandate, the money and the duty not to exclude. An NGO knows the last household and can say when a scheme is failing.
A private firm can run a logistics or a technology, under a contract that does not let profit decide who is served.
Collaboration works when the roles stay distinct and the public purpose stays with the state.

question_text: "Though the great Cholas are no more yet their name is still remembered with great pride because of their highest achievements in the domain of art and architecture." Comment. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Why the Cholas are remembered for art
topics: Why the Cholas are remembered for art
keyPointers: The dynasty is gone and the temples are not
Bronze, a wall of sculpture and a towering vimana are the achievement
The art was royal and it was also a public religion
Pride survives because the work is still in use

points.text: The Chola state ended. The reason the name is still said with pride is that its art did not.
The great temples at Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Darasuram carried a vimana and a sculpture to a height South India had not built before.
The bronzes, above all of Shiva Nataraja, joined a theology to a craft that is still recognised anywhere.
These were not private treasures. They were the centre of a living worship, which is why they were maintained.
The pride is justified by a body of work that is still standing and still in use, not by the memory of a conquest.

question_text: How far is it correct to say that the First World War was fought essentially for the preservation of the balance of power? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Was the First World War fought for the balance of power
topics: Was the First World War fought for the balance of power
subTopics: First World War and the balance of power
keyPointers: The balance of power explains the alliances, not every motive
Fear of a rising Germany sat inside that balance
Empire, nationalism and a blank cheque were also in the war
It is correct as a frame and incomplete as the whole cause

points.text: The balance of power is a large part of why 1914 became a world war. It is not the whole of why it was fought.
Two armed camps existed so that no one state could dominate Europe. The war began when that arrangement was tested and nobody would yield.
Germany's rise, Britain's fear of a continental hegemon, and Austria's fear of Serbia are balance-of-power facts.
They do not exhaust the war. National self-determination, imperial rivalry and the momentum of mobilisation were also causes.
It is correct to say the war was essentially about the balance, and necessary to add that the balance was already full of other quarrels.

question_text: How far was the Industrial Revolution in England responsible for the decline of handicrafts and cottage industries in India? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: England's industrial revolution and Indian handicrafts
topics: England's industrial revolution and Indian handicrafts
keyPointers: Cheap machine cloth undercut the Indian weaver
The damage needed a colonial market, not only a British factory
Company purchases, a tariff and the loss of a court also mattered
The revolution was the main cause and not the only one

points.text: England's industrial revolution is the largest reason Indian handicrafts declined, because it produced the cloth that replaced them.
Machine yarn and cloth entered India under a regime that kept the Indian market open and the British market closed.
The Company's earlier extraction, the end of court and temple demand, and a new taste for imports had already weakened the craftsman.
Railways then carried the import inland, so the decline was not confined to the port.
The revolution was responsible in so far as it made the competing good. Colonial power decided that India would be the market for it.

question_text: The groundwater potential of the Gangetic valley is on a serious decline. How may it affect the food security of India? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Declining Gangetic groundwater and food security
topics: Declining Gangetic groundwater and food security
keyPointers: The valley is a large share of India's grain
That grain now depends on a pump more than on the river
A falling water table means a costlier and then a smaller harvest
Food security fails as a national stock and as a local meal

points.text: The Gangetic valley feeds India, and a growing part of that feeding is groundwater that is being drawn down.
Rice and wheat in the plains are increasingly irrigated by tube wells. The water table in many blocks no longer recovers each year.
As the well deepens, the small farmer's cost rises and some land goes out of a water-heavy crop.
A regional fall in procurement would thin the national stock, and a bad monsoon would then meet a thinner ration.
Food security that rests on a declining aquifer is security with a date on it.

question_text: What are aurora australis and aurora borealis? How are these triggered? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Aurora australis and aurora borealis
topics: Aurora australis and aurora borealis
keyPointers: One is the southern lights and the other the northern
Both are the same event at opposite ends of the Earth's field
A burst from the Sun drives charged particles into that field
The colour is the atmosphere being struck, not the particle itself

points.text: Aurora borealis is the northern lights and aurora australis the southern. They are one phenomenon seen at the two magnetic poles.
The Sun throws out charged particles. When a strong stream of them reaches the Earth, the magnetic field guides them toward the polar atmosphere.
Those particles strike oxygen and nitrogen. The glow is the light those gases give off as they settle.
A more active Sun produces a wider and brighter oval, which is why the lights are sometimes seen far from the pole.
They are triggered by a solar disturbance meeting the Earth's magnetic field, and lit by the air.

question_text: What is a twister? Why are the majority of twisters observed in areas around the Gulf of Mexico? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Twisters and the Gulf of Mexico
topics: Twisters and the Gulf of Mexico
keyPointers: A twister is a violently rotating column from cloud to ground
The Gulf supplies warm moist air
Cold dry air from the continent meets it
The clash, plus a change of wind with height, spins the storm

points.text: A twister is a tornado: a narrow, violently rotating column of air between a thundercloud and the ground.
It forms inside a severe thunderstorm when winds at different heights blow differently and a rotating column is lifted until it touches down.
Around the Gulf, warm moist air from the sea meets cooler, drier air from the land, especially over the plains to the north.
That contrast is frequent and strong, and the flat land lets the storm organise, which is why this region sees most of the world's twisters.
The Gulf is the source of the warm air without which the meeting would not be violent enough.

question_text: What is regional disparity? How does it differ from diversity? How serious is the issue of regional disparity in India? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Regional disparity and diversity in India
topics: Regional disparity and diversity in India
keyPointers: Disparity is an unequal outcome. Diversity is a difference that is not itself a harm
A diverse country can be fair. A disparate one is not
India's gaps in income, health and a job are large and stubborn
The issue is serious because the same democracy contains both lives

points.text: Regional disparity is a gap in income, services and opportunity between places. Diversity is a difference of language, culture or ecology, which is not by itself a disadvantage.
A diverse region can be prosperous. A disparate one is poorer, less healthy or less employed than another, for reasons a person did not choose.
In India the gap between states, and between a city and its own hinterland, remains wide in income, learning and health.
Growth has not closed it at the speed the poorer region would need. Migration is the individual answer, and it leaves the region behind.
Diversity is a fact to live with. Disparity is a failure to correct, and in India it is serious.

question_text: Despite comprehensive policies for equity and social justice, underprivileged sections are not yet getting the full benefits of affirmative action envisaged by the Constitution. Comment. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Why affirmative action still falls short
topics: Why affirmative action still falls short
keyPointers: The Constitution envisaged a real change of condition, not only a list
The scheme reaches the person who can already reach the form
Prejudice, a weak school and a captured list leak the benefit
The policy is not a failure of intention. It is a failure of the last mile

points.text: India has written a wide affirmative action and still not delivered what the Constitution envisaged for the least advantaged.
Reservations, scholarships and a legal protection exist. They are used most by those inside the group who already have a school, a city and information.
A poor child in the same category meets a weak primary school, a hostile institution and a form he cannot fill.
Creaming within the category, and a politics of the list rather than of the outcome, keep the full benefit from arriving.
The policies are comprehensive on paper and partial in the life of the most underprivileged.

question_text: Globalization has increased urban migration by skilled, young, unmarried women from various classes. How has this trend impacted upon their personal freedom and relationship with family? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Skilled women, the city and the family
topics: Skilled women, the city and the family
keyPointers: A job in the city is a new room of one's own
Freedom of movement, money and marriage grows
The family tie stretches and is renegotiated, not simply cut
Class decides how much freedom the move actually buys

points.text: Globalisation opened urban jobs that a skilled, unmarried woman can take without a husband going first.
A salary, a rented room and a city anonymity increase her freedom of movement, of friendship and of when to marry.
The relationship with family becomes a negotiation: remittances and a video call on one side, anxiety and supervision from a distance on the other.
The freedom is larger for the woman whose class already allowed study. For others the same move can still be watched by phone.
The trend has widened personal freedom and turned the family into a relationship that must be maintained across a distance.

question_text: Critically analyse the proposition that there is a high correlation between India's cultural diversities and socio-economic marginalities. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Cultural diversity and socio-economic marginality
topics: Cultural diversity and socio-economic marginality
keyPointers: Some marginal groups are also culturally distinct, and the overlap is real
The correlation is not the same as a cause
Marginality is produced by power and land, then marked as culture
Many culturally distinct groups are not marginal, and many of the poor share the dominant culture

points.text: The proposition notices a real overlap and then explains it too quickly.
Adivasi regions, some linguistic minorities and some caste communities are both culturally distinct and poorer. That correlation can be shown.
It does not show that the culture caused the poverty. Loss of land, a remote administration and a stigma did, and the culture was then treated as the reason.
A diverse community in a city trade, or a poor community that shares the dominant culture, breaks the simple line.
The correlation is high in several regions and is not a law. Treating diversity itself as the cause of marginality is the error.
